derivations.title: Point-charge field from Gauss's law
steps: By symmetry E has the same magnitude everywhere on a sphere of radius r and points radially.
Gauss's law gives ∮E·dA=q/ε₀.
Because E is parallel to dA and constant on the sphere, the flux is E·4πr².
Set E4πr²=q/ε₀.
Therefore E=q r-hat/(4πε₀r²), with direction set by the sign of q.
derivations.interpretation: The inverse-square law follows from flux conservation plus three-dimensional spherical area growth, not from Gauss's law alone without symmetry.
derivations.unitCheck: q/(ε₀r²) has units N/C or V/m.
derivations.commonMistake: Pulling E outside the flux integral for a surface where the magnitude is not constant.
derivations.panelInterruption: Can the same Gaussian surface simplify an off-centre charge problem?
derivations.summary: Use spherical symmetry to make E constant on the Gaussian sphere, equate flux E4πr² to q/ε₀, and recover the inverse-square field.

derivations.title: Parallel-plate capacitance and stored energy
assumptions: Gap d much smaller than lateral dimensions
steps: For free surface charge density σ_f, a pillbox boundary argument gives approximately E=σ_f/ε between oppositely charged plates.
The potential difference is V=Ed=σ_fd/ε.
Total free charge is Q=σ_fA.
Capacitance C=Q/V therefore equals εA/d.
Charging work U=∫₀^Q(q/C)dq=Q²/(2C)=½CV², giving energy density u=½εE².
derivations.interpretation: Capacitance is a geometry/material property in the linear regime; inserting dielectric changes field and stored energy differently depending on fixed Q or fixed V.
derivations.unitCheck: εA/d has farad units; ½CV² has joules.
derivations.commonMistake: Using the uniform-field formula when fringing, nonlinear dielectric response, or electrode geometry dominates.
derivations.panelInterruption: What changes when the battery remains connected during dielectric insertion?
derivations.summary: Find uniform field from surface charge, integrate to voltage, form Q/V, then integrate charging work.

derivations.title: Magnetic field inside an ideal long solenoid
steps: Symmetry makes the field approximately uniform and axial inside and negligible outside the ideal long solenoid.
Choose a rectangular Amperian loop with length ℓ inside and return side outside.
Ampère's law gives ∮B·dl=μ₀I_enclosed.
Only the inside axial segment contributes appreciably, giving Bℓ.
The loop encloses nℓ turns carrying I, so Bℓ=μ₀nℓI and B=μ₀nI.
derivations.interpretation: The result is an ideal central-region approximation; a material core requires B=μH only under a suitable constitutive model.
derivations.commonMistake: Claiming the external field is exactly zero for a finite solenoid.
derivations.panelInterruption: How do finite length and a ferromagnetic core change the answer?
derivations.summary: Use a rectangular Ampère loop and the ideal inside/outside field symmetry to obtain B=μ₀nI.

derivations.title: Thin-film reflected interference condition
assumptions: Plane-parallel film of thickness t and index n
Reflection phase shifts tracked from index ordering
steps: Compare a ray reflected at the top interface with one transmitted into the film, reflected at the bottom, and returned.
The propagation optical-path difference is 2nt cosθ_t for reflected parallel rays.
Convert propagation path to phase: Δφ_prop=(2π/λ₀)2nt cosθ_t.
Add π for each reflection from a lower to a higher refractive index; only the relative number of such reversals matters.
Constructive reflection requires total Δφ=2πm and destructive reflection requires Δφ=(2m+1)π.
derivations.interpretation: The familiar bright/dark thickness formulas swap when exactly one of the two reflected amplitudes acquires a π phase reversal.
derivations.unitCheck: 2nt cosθ has length units and phase is dimensionless after division by λ₀.
derivations.commonMistake: Writing 2nt=mλ as the bright condition without checking reflection phase reversals.
derivations.panelInterruption: How do absorption, dispersion, or varying thickness change the observed colours?
derivations.summary: Compute the round-trip optical path, convert it to phase, add interface phase reversals, then impose total phase conditions.

derivations.title: Reversible adiabatic ideal-gas relation
steps: The first law is dU=δQ−P dV and δQ=0 for an adiabatic path.
For an ideal gas dU=nC_VdT, so nC_VdT=−P dV.
Use P=nRT/V to obtain C_V dT/T=−R dV/V.
Integrate: C_V lnT+R lnV=constant.
Since R=C_P−C_V and γ=C_P/C_V, obtain TV^(γ−1)=constant; combining with PV=nRT gives PV^γ=constant.
derivations.interpretation: Adiabatic alone is not enough: irreversibility generates entropy and the simple isentropic power law need not hold.
derivations.unitCheck: Logarithms apply to ratios; the conventional dimensional constant is shorthand for a relation between states.
derivations.commonMistake: Calling every adiabatic process isentropic or using Celsius temperature.
derivations.panelInterruption: How does the relation change if heat capacities depend strongly on temperature?
derivations.summary: Set heat to zero, express dU with C_V, substitute the ideal-gas equation, integrate, and use γ=C_P/C_V.

derivations.title: Small-oscillation frequency from a potential minimum
assumptions: Displacement small enough for quadratic truncation
steps: At equilibrium V'(x₀)=0 and stability requires V''(x₀)>0.
Write x=x₀+η and Taylor-expand V≈V(x₀)+½V''(x₀)η².
The force is F=−dV/dx≈−V''(x₀)η.
Newton's law gives mη-double-dot+V''(x₀)η=0.
Identify simple harmonic motion with ω₀=sqrt[V''(x₀)/m].
derivations.interpretation: Harmonic motion is a local consequence of smooth stable equilibrium; asymmetry and amplitude-dependent frequency come from higher-order terms.
derivations.unitCheck: V'' has units N/m, so V''/m has s⁻².
derivations.commonMistake: Using the approximation when V''=0 or displacement is large enough that cubic/quartic terms dominate.
derivations.panelInterruption: What happens near an unstable equilibrium or a flat-bottomed potential?
derivations.summary: Taylor-expand the potential around a stable minimum; the quadratic curvature becomes the effective spring constant.

derivations.title: Quantum harmonic-oscillator spectrum with ladder operators
assumptions: Normalized states and proper operator domains
steps: Define a=sqrt(mω/(2ħ))x+i p/sqrt(2mħω) and its adjoint a-dagger.
Use [x,p]=iħ to show [a,a-dagger]=1.
Rewrite H=ħω(a-dagger a+½)=ħω(N+½).
N=a-dagger a is positive, and ladder commutators show eigenvalues differ by integers.
A lowest state must satisfy a|0>=0, so E_n=(n+½)ħω for n=0,1,...
derivations.interpretation: Zero-point energy follows the commutator and existence of a normalizable lowest state, not a classical particle moving at ground energy.
derivations.unitCheck: ħω has energy units and ladder operators are dimensionless.
derivations.commonMistake: Assuming n can be negative or saying ground energy violates energy conservation.
derivations.panelInterruption: How do x and p matrix elements give selection rules?
derivations.summary: Factor H into ladder operators, use their commutator, require a lowest normalizable state, and build equally spaced levels.

derivations.title: Bohr-model hydrogen energy levels
assumptions: Nonrelativistic electron in circular Coulomb orbit
No spin, radiation, or relativistic corrections
steps: Balance Coulomb attraction and centripetal force: mv²/r=e²/(4πε₀r²).
Impose angular momentum mvr=nħ.
Eliminate v to obtain r_n=4πε₀ħ²n²/(me²)=a₀n².
Total energy is K+V=½mv²−e²/(4πε₀r)=−e²/(8πε₀r).
Substitute r_n to obtain E_n=−me⁴/[2(4πε₀)²ħ²n²]=−13.6 eV/n².
derivations.interpretation: The model gives correct gross hydrogen spectrum but not a valid classical orbit picture; Schrödinger theory explains states, angular momentum, degeneracy, and corrections.
derivations.commonMistake: Presenting Bohr orbits as exact quantum trajectories or applying −13.6 eV/n² to multi-electron atoms unchanged.
derivations.panelInterruption: Which observations require fine structure, Lamb shift, or reduced mass?
derivations.summary: Combine Coulomb force with angular-momentum quantization, find allowed radii, then evaluate total energy.

derivations.title: Continuity equation from local conservation
steps: The amount inside a fixed volume is Q=∫_Vρ dV.
Local conservation says its rate of decrease equals outward boundary flux: dQ/dt=−∮_∂V J·n dA.
Move the time derivative inside: ∫_V ∂ρ/∂t dV=−∮J·n dA.
Use Gauss's theorem on the flux term.
Because the volume is arbitrary, ∂ρ/∂t+∇·J=0 pointwise.
derivations.interpretation: The same structure describes charge, probability, mass, and other locally conserved quantities when the correct density and flux are used.
derivations.unitCheck: Both ∂ρ/∂t and divergence J have density/time units.
derivations.commonMistake: Using the source-free equation when production, loss, reactions, or moving control volumes are present.
derivations.panelInterruption: How is a source term or moving boundary included?
derivations.summary: Write integral conservation for an arbitrary fixed volume, convert boundary flux to volume divergence, and equate integrands.

derivations.title: Diffusion equation from Fick's law
steps: Start from continuity: ∂c/∂t+∇·J=0.
Use Fick's first law J=−D∇c.
Substitute to get ∂c/∂t−∇·(D∇c)=0.
For constant D, simplify ∇·(D∇c)=D∇²c.
Therefore ∂c/∂t=D∇²c.
derivations.interpretation: Diffusion smooths concentration gradients and has characteristic length sqrt(Dt); anisotropic or concentration-dependent D changes the operator.
derivations.unitCheck: D has m²/s, so D∇²c has concentration/time units.
derivations.commonMistake: Using constant-D diffusion in systems with reactions, drift, advection, or anomalous transport.
derivations.panelInterruption: What boundary conditions represent no flux or a fixed concentration?
derivations.summary: Combine local conservation with Fick's gradient-driven flux and simplify for constant diffusivity.

derivations.title: Heat equation from energy conservation and Fourier's law
assumptions: Constant density ρ_m, heat capacity c_p, conductivity k
steps: Thermal energy density change is ρ_m c_p ∂T/∂t.
Energy conservation gives ρ_m c_p ∂T/∂t=−∇·q.
Fourier's law is q=−k∇T.
Substitute to obtain ρ_m c_p ∂T/∂t=∇·(k∇T).
For constant k, ∂T/∂t=α∇²T with thermal diffusivity α=k/(ρ_m c_p).
derivations.interpretation: Temperature disturbances spread diffusively with scale sqrt(αt); radiation, convection, contact resistance, and temperature-dependent properties require added terms.
derivations.unitCheck: α has m²/s and α∇²T has K/s.
derivations.commonMistake: Confusing thermal conductivity k with diffusivity α or ignoring boundary heat transfer.
derivations.panelInterruption: How would a volumetric heat source or radiative boundary modify the model?
derivations.summary: Apply local energy conservation to Fourier heat flux and identify thermal diffusivity.

derivations.title: Monostatic radar range equation scaling
assumptions: Matched polarization and stated losses omitted initially
Antenna gain G used on transmit and receive
steps: Power density at target is S_t=P_tG/(4πR²).
The target reradiates an equivalent power toward radar described by radar cross section σ, giving return power density S_r=S_tσ/(4πR²).
The receiving antenna effective aperture is A_e=Gλ²/(4π).
Received power is P_r=S_rA_e.
Combine factors: P_r=P_tG²λ²σ/[(4π)³R⁴], then include system losses/noise separately.
derivations.interpretation: The R⁻⁴ scaling comes from outward and return geometric spreading; detectability also depends on noise, waveform, integration, probability criteria, atmosphere, clutter, and losses.
derivations.unitCheck: Power density W/m² times σ m² times aperture m² divided by spreading area m² returns W.
derivations.commonMistake: Treating radar cross section as physical area or using the equation without far-field, loss, noise, and detection assumptions.
derivations.panelInterruption: How do coherent integration and bandwidth enter detection without changing basic geometric scaling?
derivations.summary: Apply transmit spreading, target reradiation via σ, return spreading, and receive effective aperture to obtain R⁻⁴ power.

derivations.title: Telescope light-gathering and diffraction scaling
assumptions: Same throughput when comparing ideal apertures
steps: Collected incident power is irradiance times aperture area A=πD²/4, so light-gathering scales as D².
The far-field amplitude is the Fourier transform of the circular pupil.
Its Airy pattern first zero occurs at sinθ≈1.22λ/D for small angles.
Thus angular diffraction scale decreases as 1/D while collected photon rate increases as D².
Real sensitivity additionally includes throughput, background, detector noise, atmosphere, exposure, and sampling.
derivations.interpretation: Light gathering and resolution are distinct benefits of aperture; magnification alone provides neither.
derivations.unitCheck: λ/D is dimensionless angle in radians; area has m².
derivations.commonMistake: Equating pixel count or magnification with optical resolution and ignoring central obstruction/seeing.
derivations.panelInterruption: How do atmosphere and detector sampling change practical resolution and sensitivity?
derivations.summary: Aperture area gives D² photon collection, while circular-pupil diffraction gives angular scale approximately 1.22λ/D.

derivations.title: Inverse-variance weighted mean from Gaussian likelihood
assumptions: Independent measurements x_i of one common value μ
steps: The likelihood is proportional to product exp[−(x_i−μ)²/(2u_i²)].
Maximizing likelihood is minimizing χ²(μ)=Σ(x_i−μ)²/u_i².
Differentiate: dχ²/dμ=−2Σ(x_i−μ)/u_i²=0.
Solve μ_hat=Σw_ix_i/Σw_i with w_i=1/u_i².
The curvature or direct propagation gives u(μ_hat)=1/sqrt(Σw_i).
derivations.interpretation: More precise independent measurements receive larger weight, but underestimated uncertainty or hidden correlation can dominate and make the result misleading.
derivations.unitCheck: Weights have inverse-square measurement units; weighted ratio returns measurement units.
derivations.commonMistake: Using inverse-variance weights when measurements disagree beyond stated uncertainties or share calibration bias.
derivations.panelInterruption: How would you include covariance or between-study heterogeneity?
derivations.summary: Write the independent Gaussian likelihood, minimize chi-square, solve the normal equation, and read uncertainty from total weight.
